nodes.name: Cheyenne
nodes.fact: Wyoming's capital and largest city began in 1867 as a junction on the Union Pacific Railroad and was named for the Cheyenne people. Its Frontier Days is billed as the world's largest outdoor rodeo and western festival.
nodes.legend: A man at the rodeo grounds wants to sell you a saddle, a canoe and 'half a vending machine,' cash only, no questions. He asks you several questions.

nodes.name: Laramie
nodes.fact: Home of the University of Wyoming, Laramie sits at 7,220 feet. In 1870 women here became the first in the world to serve on a jury, and Louisa Swain became the first woman in the United States to cast a legal vote in a general election.
nodes.legend: At 7,220 feet one beer counts as three, which locals call 'value'. A man in a bathrobe explains that his lawn flamingos are federal informants.

nodes.name: Medicine Bow
nodes.fact: A town of a few hundred people at most, and the setting of Owen Wister's novel The Virginian. The Virginian Hotel was built in 1911, and early fossil hunters dug dinosaurs at nearby Como Bluff.
nodes.legend: The population sign is updated by hand, and today it says 'depends if Randy comes back.' Randy went for cigarettes during a previous administration.

nodes.name: Rawlins
nodes.fact: Named for Union General John A. Rawlins, who camped here in 1867. The Wyoming State Penitentiary is here, and a red pigment mined nearby, 'Rawlins Red', is thought to have been the Brooklyn Bridge's original paint.
nodes.legend: Three separate people tell you they're 'between ankle monitors right now.' The wind takes your hat, your receipt, and one of your better opinions.

nodes.name: Rock Springs
nodes.fact: A coal town named for a spring that mining later dried up. Immigrants arrived from so many countries that locals called it the '57 Variety Town'.
nodes.legend: A gentleman at the truck stop is disassembling a vending machine 'to see how it thinks.' He has been at it since the weekend and has fourteen parts left over.

nodes.name: Evanston
nodes.fact: A county seat near the Utah line, founded in 1868 as a divisional point on the transcontinental railroad. It is usually said to be named for James A. Evans, a Union Pacific engineer.
nodes.legend: Half the parking lot has crossed the border for lottery tickets, the other half for fireworks. One truck did both and no longer has eyebrows.

nodes.name: Kemmerer
nodes.fact: James Cash Penney opened his first Golden Rule Store here in 1902, the start of the J. C. Penney chain. Fossil Butte National Monument lies to the west.
nodes.legend: A local offers to sell you a 50-million-year-old fossil fish. It still smells like a 50-hour-old fish.

nodes.name: Farson
nodes.fact: This crossing of the Big Sandy River was a Pony Express and stagecoach station. An archaeological site nearby holds the remains of more than 200 pronghorn from communal hunts.
nodes.legend: The only traffic is a man on a riding mower doing a brisk 11 mph toward Rock Springs. His license is suspended and his schedule is wide open.

nodes.name: Pinedale
nodes.fact: A gateway to the Wind River Range and home of the Museum of the Mountain Man. Its Green River Rendezvous re-creates the fur trade's big trading gatherings.
nodes.legend: You can't tell the historical reenactors from the guys who just dress like that. Asking is considered rude, and in one case, dangerous to your jerky.

nodes.name: Jackson
nodes.fact: Often called Jackson Hole, after the surrounding valley named for trapper David Jackson. The town square is famous for arches made of elk antlers.
nodes.legend: A sandwich costs forty dollars and comes with a story about the sourdough. Your party's combined net worth is asked politely to wait outside.

nodes.label: Grand Teton
nodes.name: Grand Teton National Park
nodes.fact: Established in 1929 and greatly expanded in 1950 after John D. Rockefeller Jr. donated land. The Grand Teton rises to 13,775 feet.
nodes.legend: Dwayne texts: 'those mountains look fake.' You haven't told him where you are. You are going to check the truck for trackers.

nodes.label: South Entrance
nodes.name: Yellowstone: South Entrance
nodes.fact: Signed into law by President Grant in 1872, Yellowstone was the first U.S. national park and is widely considered the world's first. It holds well over half of the world's geysers and hydrothermal features.
nodes.legend: The ranger asks if you have anything to declare. Your whole party looks at the cooler. The cooler, wisely, says nothing.

nodes.label: East Entrance
nodes.name: Yellowstone: East Entrance
nodes.fact: The park's eastern gateway, reached by highway from Cody. Inside, the 1870 Washburn Expedition named the Old Faithful geyser for its regular eruptions.
nodes.legend: You made it. Aunt Tammy's only advice was 'don't pet the fluffy cows,' and she has the scar to back it up.

nodes.name: Wheatland
nodes.fact: A farm town built on irrigation: an 1883 system with a 2,380-foot tunnel watered the Wheatland Flats. The local irrigation district is described as the largest privately owned system in the country.
nodes.legend: A man insists he can taste the difference between ditch water and tap water. Nobody asked him to prove it. He is proving it.

nodes.name: Fort Laramie
nodes.fact: Founded as the fur-trading post Fort William in 1834 and bought by the U.S. Army in 1849, it was a major stop on the Oregon Trail. The fort was decommissioned in 1890.
nodes.legend: A volunteer in wool uniform offers you 1850s medicine. It's mostly whiskey, which makes it the most responsible thing anyone has offered you all week.

nodes.name: Register Cliff
nodes.fact: Oregon Trail emigrants carved their names into this sandstone cliff, often while camped a day west of Fort Laramie. It is one of three famous 'registers' in Wyoming.
nodes.legend: Among the pioneer names you find 'DWAYNE WUZ HERE', very fresh. He is supposed to be under house arrest.

nodes.name: Douglas
nodes.fact: Home of the Wyoming State Fair and officially the 'Home of the Jackalope', a legend credited to local taxidermist Douglas Herrick. Sir Barton, the first Triple Crown winner, is buried here.
nodes.legend: A man in camo offers a guided jackalope hunt for $60 and a ride to his storage unit. You buy a postcard instead and feel you've grown as a person.

nodes.name: Casper
nodes.fact: Wyoming's second-largest city, nicknamed 'The Oil City', sits on the North Platte River. Its name comes from Fort Caspar, honoring Lieutenant Caspar Collins; the spelling drifted.
nodes.legend: The wind is so steady that locals who visit calm places fall over. A pawn shop is selling nine leaf blowers, all 'found.'

nodes.name: Independence Rock
nodes.fact: A granite dome about 130 feet high and a landmark on the Oregon, California and Mormon trails. Emigrants hoped to reach it by July 4 to beat the mountain snows, and many carved their names on it.
nodes.legend: Alex climbs it in flip-flops and announces a new personal philosophy at the top. It does not survive the climb down.

nodes.name: Muddy Gap
nodes.fact: A tiny unincorporated community beside a natural gap that Muddy Creek flows through. It is a lonely crossroads on the way across central Wyoming.
nodes.legend: The gas station is also the post office, the bait shop, and Earl. Earl does not recommend the sushi, and Earl made the sushi.

nodes.name: Lander
nodes.fact: In 1906 Lander became the western end of the Chicago and North Western's 'Cowboy Line', giving it the slogan 'where rails end and trails begin' (the trains quit in 1972). The National Outdoor Leadership School (NOLS) was founded here and is headquartered in town.
nodes.legend: Where trails end and rails begin, or at least where the side-by-side trails and hippy NOLS types hang out. Your cousin Dwayne sees you off. He has been awake since Tuesday, has alphabetized the gravel in your driveway, and swears it's just allergy medicine.

nodes.name: Sinks Canyon
nodes.fact: A state park southwest of Lander, named for where the Middle Fork of the Popo Agie River flows into a limestone cavern, 'the Sinks', and comes back up a quarter-mile down the canyon in a pool called 'the Rise'. Dye tests show the underground trip takes over two hours.
nodes.legend: A woman in a hemp poncho says the river goes underground to think about what you've done. It comes back up two hours later, still unimpressed.

nodes.name: South Pass City
nodes.fact: An 1867 gold strike swelled this town to about 2,000 people within a year; by the mid-1870s about 100 remained. Esther Hobart Morris became the first female justice of the peace in the U.S. here in 1870.
nodes.legend: It's a ghost town, but the ghosts moved out over the noise from a guy 'prospecting' with a leaf blower at 3 a.m.

nodes.name: Riverton
nodes.fact: Founded in 1906 and named for the rivers that meet here. It hosts a National Weather Service office covering western and central Wyoming.
nodes.legend: The forecast calls for sun, hail, and a man selling a hot tub out of a horse trailer. All three arrive early.

nodes.name: Shoshoni
nodes.fact: Named for the Shoshone people, this small town sits where U.S. 20 and U.S. 26 meet, once together called the Yellowstone Highway. Boysen Reservoir is close by.
nodes.legend: Every third building is vacant and the others are 'vacant-curious.' A raccoon appears to be running the car wash, and running it well.

nodes.name: Thermopolis
nodes.fact: Its name is Greek for 'hot city'. The town claims the world's largest mineral hot spring, and an 1896 treaty with the Shoshone and Arapaho keeps public bathing free.
nodes.legend: You soak next to a man who says this is his first bath since the Super Bowl. He doesn't say which one.

nodes.name: Worland
nodes.fact: A county seat on the Big Horn River in the Bighorn Basin, with a reputation as Wyoming's least windy town.
nodes.legend: With no wind to blame, locals have to take responsibility for their trampolines being in the road. Morale is fragile.

nodes.name: Ten Sleep
nodes.fact: The name records distance in 'sleeps': it was ten days' travel from Fort Laramie, from Yellowstone, and from an Indian agency in Montana.
nodes.legend: Dwayne calls this place 'Zero Sleep' for personal reasons and is not welcome at the motel.

nodes.name: Dubois
nodes.fact: Pronounced DOO-boyz. Traces of the Mountain Shoshone surround the town, 'tie hacks' once cut railroad ties in the nearby mountains, and a large bighorn sheep herd winters close by.
nodes.legend: A bighorn sheep stands in the road, makes eye contact, and demands your jerky. Pay him. The last guy didn't, and his tailgate is now 'abstract.'

nodes.name: Buffalo
nodes.fact: A county seat at the foot of the Bighorn Mountains. It was at the center of the 1892 Johnson County War between big cattle outfits and small ranchers.
nodes.legend: A bar regular offers to show you his belt buckle collection. He is wearing all of them. He clanks when he breathes.

nodes.name: Sheridan
nodes.fact: Named for Union General Philip Sheridan. Buffalo Bill Cody auditioned performers for his Wild West show from the porch of the Sheridan Inn, and the WYO Rodeo dates to 1931.
nodes.legend: You audition for a Wild West show from the same porch. There is no show. A nice couple gives you two dollars to stop.

nodes.name: Gillette
nodes.fact: The self-styled 'Energy Capital of the Nation', surrounded by coal, oil and gas fields. Once called Donkey Town, it was renamed for railroad surveyor Edward Gillette.
nodes.legend: Every pickup is lifted so high the drivers need oxygen. One has a ladder, a flag, and a restraining order from a drive-thru.

nodes.name: Devils Tower
nodes.fact: Sacred to many Plains tribes and also known as Bear Lodge, it became the first U.S. national monument in 1906. In 1941 a stunt parachutist landed on top and was stranded for six days.
nodes.legend: Dwayne is convinced the aliens are coming back and has built them a welcome casserole. It has been in his glovebox since June.

nodes.name: Cody
nodes.fact: Founded in 1896 with help from William 'Buffalo Bill' Cody, who named the Irma Hotel for his daughter. Cody calls itself the 'Rodeo Capital of the World'.
nodes.legend: A rodeo clown recruits you on sight. You'd be flattered, but he says it's because you already have the face and the lack of insurance.
